headline: A two-speed global economy: strong AI demand, uneven domestic growth
dek: Across the United States, China, Japan, and South Korea, markets are balancing resilient technology demand against inflation, currency pressure, and weaker traditional activity.
story_title: AI investment is booming—but the wider economy is not moving in lockstep
story_html:
United States 🇺🇸 The latest U.S. labor-market figures point to an economy that still has considerable momentum. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than twice the consensus expectation, while unemployment edged down to 4.1%. Average hourly earnings also accelerated. The report strengthens the argument that the Federal Reserve may need to keep interest rates higher for longer—or even consider another increase—because demand remains firm while inflation is still above target. Yet the composition of growth matters: investment linked to artificial intelligence and data centers is supporting activity, even as households continue to feel pressure from elevated prices. ([fidelity.com](https://www.fidelity.com/news/article/us-economy/202611060844RTRSNEWSCOMBINED_KCN3WH1WQ-OUSBS_1?utm_source=openai))

China 🇨🇳 China presents a more uneven picture. Factory activity weakened in October, with new export orders slipping into contraction, reflecting softer conventional manufacturing demand and the continuing drag from the property downturn. At the same time, the People’s Bank of China is managing a stronger renminbi after robust exports and large trade surpluses pushed the currency higher. Its decision to raise the foreign-exchange reserve requirement ratio from 4% to 6% is designed to moderate one-sided appreciation rather than signal a dramatic change in interest-rate policy. China is therefore not simply slowing; it is attempting to redirect growth toward advanced manufacturing, services, and other newer drivers. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/f1e0e24004da425a1b3c8935b16a245c?utm_source=openai))

Japan 🇯🇵 Japan is receiving a different kind of policy signal. Real wages rose for a ninth consecutive month in September, increasing the likelihood that the Bank of Japan will continue normalizing monetary policy. Nominal wages climbed 4.6%, their fastest pace since 1997, suggesting that the country may be moving closer to a sustained wage–price cycle after decades of deflationary pressure. However, higher energy costs, a weaker yen, and strong prices for semiconductors connected to global AI demand are also adding to inflation. The BOJ must therefore judge whether price increases reflect healthy income growth or an externally imposed cost shock. ([ca.marketscreener.com](https://ca.marketscreener.com/news/japan-s-real-wages-rise-for-ninth-month-in-september-backing-boj-rate-hike-ce785fdddd8bf324?utm_source=openai))

South Korea 🇰🇷 South Korea is the clearest beneficiary of the AI investment wave. October exports reached a record $115.3 billion, up 93.7% year on year, while semiconductor exports surged 259% to $56.4 billion. Shipments to both China and the United States rose sharply, showing how Korean producers sit inside several crucial technology supply chains. The strength may give the Bank of Korea more room to tighten policy, but it also exposes a vulnerability: roughly half of the export surge came from chips. The common theme across the four economies is not synchronized growth. It is a widening split between AI-related capital spending, which remains powerful, and older sources of demand—property, ordinary manufacturing, and household purchasing power—which are much less robust. ([m-en.yna.co.kr](https://m-en.yna.co.kr/view/AEN20261101000952320?section=economy-finance%2Feconomy&utm_source=openai))
b2_summary: The four economies are growing at different speeds. The United States has a strong labor market, partly supported by AI and data-center investment. China’s exports remain important, but factory activity and domestic demand are weaker, especially because of the property downturn. Japan is seeing stronger wages, which may allow the Bank of Japan to raise rates. South Korea is benefiting strongly from demand for memory chips used in AI infrastructure. The shared theme is an uneven recovery: technology investment is powerful, but traditional manufacturing, housing, and consumer spending are less healthy.

vocabulary.meaning: Strong enough to continue despite problems or pressure (회복력이 있는, 탄력적인).
The average prediction made by economists or analysts (시장 예상치, 컨센서스 전망).
A period when economic activity or production decreases (경제 위축, 수축).
A sustained fall in activity and prices in the real-estate market (부동산 경기 하강, 부동산 침체).
The share of foreign-currency deposits that banks must keep at the central bank (외화 지급준비율).
To move interest rates and other policies back toward more typical levels after an unusual period (통화정책 정상화).
A process in which higher wages raise prices, and higher prices lead workers to demand higher wages (임금·물가 순환).
The network of companies and countries involved in producing and delivering a product (공급망).
A currency rising mainly in one direction, often too quickly for policymakers’ comfort (일방적 통화 절상).

common_theme: AI-led investment is strong, but traditional demand is uneven: the United States and South Korea benefit from technology spending, while China faces weaker conventional manufacturing and Japan balances wage growth against imported inflation.

concept.title: Monetary policy transmission
concept.explanation: This is the process through which a central bank’s decisions affect borrowing costs, exchange rates, investment, employment, and prices. For example, a rate hike can make loans more expensive, reduce demand, and eventually slow inflation.

quiz.question: Why might strong South Korean semiconductor exports give the Bank of Korea more room to raise interest rates?
options: They can support national income and growth, making higher rates less damaging in the short term.
They force the U.S. Federal Reserve to cut rates.
quiz.explanation: Strong exports can support growth and corporate income, allowing the central bank to focus more on inflation and financial stability.

one_sentence: The world economy is not moving as one machine: AI investment is accelerating, while housing, ordinary manufacturing, and household purchasing power remain uneven.
